verdict.rationale: FireHydrant documents an official command-line tool, `fhcli`, built to submit changes from existing CI or orchestration systems such as Jenkins. Headless automation is further backed by token-authenticated API keys that cover "anything you can do on the FireHydrant UI" and by bot tokens for machine identities. However, the documented scope of fhcli is narrow: it records change events like Docker image creation, deploys and build statuses, not full headless operation of the product. missing for 10: documentation of fhcli commands beyond change-event recording, CI usage examples or a CI integration guide for broader incident and runbook automation, and independent or hands-on corroboration of CI use.

support.subject: As an AI-native user, I can run the product headlessly / in CI for automation

citations.quote: FireHydrant provides a command line tool, `fhcli`, to easily submit changes from your existing CI or orchestration systems.
You can use fhcli to record the creation of Docker images, deploy events in Jenkins, CI build statuses, etc.
You can use the FireHydrant API to configure integrations, define incidents, and set up webhooks--anything you can do on the FireHydrant UI.
FireHydrant supports bot tokens to act on behalf of a computer instead of a user's account.
